title: Nonderogatory → Cyclic Vector (Finite Field Version)
description: Weakens the infinite field hypothesis to |K| > n: over a field K with |K| > n, every nonderogatory matrix has a cyclic vector. Uses a finite version of the union avoidance lemma.

meta.author: Based on classical union avoidance argument
meta.assumptions: None. Fully verified with 0 axioms and 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext: The rational canonical form theorem (dating to the 19th-century work of Weierstrass, Jordan, and Frobenius on canonical forms for matrices over fields) implies that a matrix is nonderogatory — has minimal polynomial equal to characteristic polynomial — if and only if it is similar to the companion matrix of its characteristic polynomial, equivalently if the module $K^n$ (viewed as a $K[X]$-module via $M$) is cyclic, generated by a single element. The existence of such a cyclic generator (called a 'cyclic vector') is therefore equivalent to nonderogatory: the two conditions are the same. Over infinite fields, the proof uses the union avoidance lemma (attributed to various sources; see van der Waerden's *Modern Algebra* for the classical statement): a finite union of proper subspaces cannot cover an infinite-dimensional vector space, since on any line through a bad point, only finitely many points are 'bad'. The finite-field version sharpens this: the line argument shows at most 1 bad scalar per subspace, so $|K| > k$ suffices for $k$ subspaces. The connection to computational algebra and coding theory is significant: cyclic linear codes (Reed-Solomon, BCH) over finite fields $\text{GF}(q)$ correspond precisely to cyclic modules, and the generator polynomial is the analog of the cyclic vector. The bound $|K| > n$ matches the degree of the minimal polynomial, reflecting the number of scalar-avoidance constraints in the proof.
overview.problemStatement: Over a field K with |K| > n, if M ∈ M_n(K) is nonderogatory (minpoly = charpoly), then M has a cyclic vector.
overview.text: Weakens the infinite field hypothesis to |K| > n for the nonderogatory → cyclic vector theorem, using a finite version of the union avoidance lemma.
overview.proofStrategy:
Follows the infinite field proof structure:
1. Factor the minimal polynomial μ into irreducible factors
2. For each factor q, define the kernel of (μ/q)(M) as a proper subspace
3. Apply finite union avoidance (|K| > n ≥ number of factors) to find v outside all kernels
4. Show v is cyclic using the GCD argument
keyInsights: The classical infinite-field proof uses 'infinitely many elements, so avoid finitely many bad scalars on a line'; the finite version replaces this with a counting argument: at most k bad scalars per subspace, so k < |K| suffices
The bound k ≤ n (number of irreducible factors ≤ degree of μ) is proved by the fact that each irreducible has degree ≥ 1 and the product of normalized factors equals μ — a degree-sum argument

The contradiction in Phase 4 uses a divisibility chain: v ∉ ker((μ/q)(M)) for all normalized factors q, but the GCD argument produces exactly such a kernel membership — the union avoidance and the cyclic witness are precisely calibrated to each other

The three helper lemmas (aeval_ne_zero, gcd_aeval, ker_ne_top) are reused unchanged from the infinite field version — only the union avoidance lemma itself changes, demonstrating clean separation of concerns in the proof architecture
This proof works over any [Fintype K] field with |K| > n, which includes all finite fields GF(q) for large enough q — covering essentially all finite-field applications of the cyclic vector theorem

sections.mathContext: Bézout: $\gcd(p,\mu) = A\cdot p + B\cdot\mu$ (EuclideanDomain.gcd_eq_gcd_ab). If $p(M)v=0$ and $\mu(M)=0$ (Cayley-Hamilton): $\gcd(p,\mu)(M)v = A(M)(p(M)v) + B(M)(\mu(M)v) = 0$. These three lemmas are identical to the infinite field version (OQ-05-OQ-01) — only the union avoidance lemma changes.

sections.title: Main Theorem Phases 1–2: Factor Collection and Proper Subspaces
sections.summary: Phase 1 (lines 223-274): collect normalized irreducible factors of μ into Finset nf using normalizedFactors. Phase 1.5: prove |nf| ≤ n (each irreducible has degree ≥ 1, sum of degrees = n = deg μ). This connects |K| > n to the union avoidance requirement |K| > |nf|. Phase 2 (lines 275-311): define proper subspaces S(q) = ker((μ/q)(M)) for each q ∈ nf, and prove S(q) ≠ ⊤ using aeval_ne_zero_of_ne_zero (deg(μ/q) < n).
sections.mathContext: For nonderogatory $M$: $\mu_M = \chi_M$ has degree $n$. Factors $q_1,\ldots,q_k$ satisfy $\sum \deg q_i = n$ and $\deg q_i \ge 1$, so $k \le n < |K|$. Each $S(q_i) = \ker((\mu/q_i)(M))$ is a proper subspace since $\deg(\mu/q_i) = n - \deg q_i < n$ and $\mu/q_i \ne 0$ by minimality.

sections.title: Main Theorem Phases 3–4: Union Avoidance and Cyclic Vector
sections.summary: Phase 3 (lines 312-314): apply not_union_proper_subspaces_fin with the proper subspaces S(q) to get v outside all of them. Phase 4 (lines 315-358): show v is cyclic by contradiction. If p(M)v = 0 with p ≠ 0, deg p < n, let d = gcd(p,μ); then d(M)v = 0 by gcd_aeval. Since d | μ = d·s, find q₀ | s (irreducible); then μ/q₀ = d·t, so (μ/q₀)(M)v = 0, placing v ∈ S(q₀) — contradicting v ∉ S(q₀). Lines 360-362 close the namespace and section.
sections.mathContext: Divisibility chain: $d \mid \mu$, $\mu = d \cdot s$; pick irreducible $q' \mid s$ (via exists_mem_normalizedFactors_of_dvd); then $\mu = q' \cdot (d \cdot t)$ so $\mu/q' = d \cdot t$; thus $(\mu/q')(M)v = t(M) \cdot d(M)v = 0$, placing $v \in S(q')$, contradicting $v \notin S(q')$ from Phase 3.

conclusion.summary: The nonderogatory → cyclic vector theorem is proved for fields with $|K| > n$, strictly weakening the [Infinite K] hypothesis of the parent proof. The proof is complete with 0 axioms and 0 sorries, using the finite union avoidance lemma with explicit cardinality control.
conclusion.implications: This formalization gives the tightest known purely combinatorial condition for the existence of cyclic vectors over finite fields. The sharp bound $|K| > n$ matches the number of irreducible factors of $\mu_M$, and the proof technique (line argument + counting) is adaptable to other union avoidance applications in computational algebra and coding theory. Together with the infinite field version (OQ-05-OQ-01), this completes a two-case analysis covering all fields.
openQuestions: Is the bound $|K| > n$ tight in the sense that for every $n$ and every field $K$ with $|K| \le n$, there exists a nonderogatory $M \in M_n(K)$ with no cyclic vector? If so, can this lower bound example be formalized?
Can the condition be tightened to $|K| > k$ where $k$ is the number of distinct irreducible factors of $\mu_M$ (which may be much less than $n$ for sparse minimal polynomials)?

The Chevalley-Warning theorem provides a different finite field cardinality-based existence argument. Is there a connection between the union avoidance approach here and the polynomial method used in Chevalley-Warning?

crossReferences.description: Parent: nonderogatory → cyclic vector for [Infinite K]. This file weakens [Infinite K] to |K| > n, making the result applicable to finite fields GF(q) with q > n.
Parent of the OQ-05 chain: minimal polynomial reduction in general K-algebras. The cyclic vector theorem is a key application of the minimal polynomial theory.
Cyclic vectors have full Lebesgue measure — a complementary density result showing that cyclic vectors are 'almost everywhere' in the space.

Root proof: Cayley-Hamilton theorem — characteristic polynomial annihilates the matrix. The nonderogatory condition (minpoly = charpoly) is the equality case connecting Cayley-Hamilton to the cyclic vector theory.
